t: Find the Maximum Sequence Value of Array
o: Pick exactly 2k elements, split the chosen subsequence into a first half of k and a second half of k (in index order), and maximize OR(first half) XOR OR(second half). With n ≤ 400 and k ≤ 200, checking all subsequences is impossible, but values fit in 7 bits. Key observation: only the OR of each half matters, so we can precompute, for every prefix, the best achievable OR using exactly c elements — and likewise for every suffix — then combine at every split point.
k: OR is monotone under adding elements, so 'max OR with exactly c picks from a prefix' is a simple DP: dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c-1] | x).
Precompute prefix DP and suffix DP (on the reversed array); the answer is max over split i of prefix[i][k] XOR suffix[n-i][k].
Values < 2^7 keep all OR/XOR operations cheap and bounded.

a.i: Enumerate all index combinations of size 2k, OR the first k and last k, XOR them. Only feasible for tiny inputs but establishes the baseline.
s: OR first k and last k separately
a.t: Exponential — C(n, 2k) combinations; only viable for tiny n

a.i: P[i][c] = maximum OR using exactly c elements among the first i; S[i][c] same on the last i. Both satisfy P[i+1][c] = max(P[i][c], P[i][c-1] | nums[i]). Every candidate answer splits the array at some i, taking k from each side, so scanning all splits gives the optimum.
s: Build prefix table P with the recurrence P[i+1][c] = max(P[i][c], P[i][c-1] | x)
Build suffix table S identically on the reversed array
Answer = max over i in [k, n-k] of P[i][k] XOR S[n-i][k]
a.t: O(n²k) — two DP tables of n×k transitions each, plus an O(n) combine scan

w: Always present the DP: the brute force signals understanding but cannot run. Pitfalls: forgetting the split must leave at least k elements on each side, and confusing 'exactly k' with 'at most k' (exactly is required since the subsequence has size 2k). Follow-up: how would you adapt if halves had different sizes? Just parameterize c on each side and scan all (c, k-c) splits.
